cards.title: MLOps: The Operational Discipline for ML Systems
cards.teaser: MLOps is the intersection of Machine Learning, Software Engineering, and Operations. It is what happens when you take DevOps discipline — automation, versioning, monitoring, continuous delivery — and apply it to the full lifecycle of a machine learning system, from data to model to serving infrastructure.

runs.text: The term MLOps emerged around 2017–2018 as practitioners at companies like Google, Uber, and Netflix recognized that getting ML models into production reliably was a distinct engineering problem — not solved by data science tooling alone, and not solved by conventional DevOps tooling alone.

A minimal definition: MLOps is the set of practices that unify ML system development (Dev) and ML system operation (Ops). Its goals are to shorten the time from training to production, to improve the reliability of deployed models, and to enable rapid iteration while keeping systems trustworthy.
MLOps inherits three distinct disciplines:

items.text: — continuous integration and delivery, infrastructure-as-code, automated testing, version control, and fast feedback loops.

— service-level objectives (SLOs), observability (metrics, logs, traces), error budgets, and runbook culture. The SRE principle that reliability is a feature, not an afterthought, applies fully to ML systems.

— feature engineering pipelines, experiment tracking, model versioning, hyperparameter management, and the particular challenges of data-dependent software (data drift, concept drift, training-serving skew).

runs.text: Chip Huyen's Designing Machine Learning Systems (2022) defines MLOps as: "a set of tools and best practices for bringing ML into production." Andriy Burkov's Machine Learning Engineering (2020) frames the same territory as the engineering complement to data science — everything required to make a trained model useful in the real world.

MLOps is the practice of running ML systems like you would run production software — with automation, monitoring, versioning, and reliability engineering — rather than like a research experiment that happens to be deployed.

cards.title: The ML Production Gap: 87% Never Deploy
cards.teaser: Industry surveys consistently report that roughly 87% of machine learning models never make it to production. The models work in notebooks. They fail in deployment. Understanding why is the founding motivation for MLOps as a discipline.

runs.text: The 87% statistic — first widely circulated by VentureBeat in 2019 citing data from Gartner, and corroborated by multiple subsequent practitioner surveys — captures a specific failure mode: the gap between a model that performs well in a research environment and a model that reliably serves predictions in a production system.
The gap is not a model quality problem. Models that fail to deploy are often technically sound. They fail to deploy because of:

items.text: The model was trained in a Jupyter notebook on a GPU workstation. Production runs on a containerized CPU service. The dependencies differ. The runtime differs. The latency requirements were never specified.
Nobody built an API endpoint, a feature store integration, or a request-handling layer. The model exists as a file with no mechanism to receive production inputs.
The data scientist who built the model moved to the next project. No engineer owns the deployment. The model sits in an artifact store, waiting for a handoff that never happens.

Even models that are deployed are often never monitored. Without monitoring, a model whose performance has decayed is indistinguishable from a working model — until someone notices wrong outputs downstream.

runs.text: The 87% number should be understood as a diagnosis, not just a statistic. Every percentage point represents an ML project that consumed data science time, compute, and organizational capital without delivering value. MLOps exists to close this gap.

Most ML models never reach production — not because they are bad models, but because nobody built the infrastructure to run them, serve them, or monitor them once deployed. MLOps is the discipline that fixes this.

cards.title: Why ML Is Harder Than Software
cards.teaser: In traditional software, code is code and behavior is deterministic. In ML systems, data is code, behavior is statistical, and the system can degrade silently over time without any change to the codebase. These three properties make ML systems uniquely hard to operate.

runs.text: A conventional software system fails loudly: an exception is thrown, a health check fails, a latency SLO is breached. An ML system can fail silently: the service stays up, predictions are returned on time, and accuracy quietly erodes as the world changes around a frozen model.
Three properties distinguish ML systems from traditional software:

items.text: In software, behavior is determined by source code. In ML, behavior is determined jointly by source code and training data. Changing the data changes the model's behavior — without touching a line of code. This means data must be versioned, validated, and managed with the same rigor as code. It rarely is.

A deployed software service does not get worse over time if you don't touch it. A deployed ML model does — because the real-world distribution it was trained on shifts. A recommendation model trained in January will perform differently in December. This is called concept drift (the relationship between inputs and outputs changes) or data drift (the input distribution changes). Neither triggers an error. Both degrade user outcomes.

Training is non-deterministic (random seeds, floating-point order, distributed training). Inference can be non-deterministic (sampling, dropout at inference time). This makes debugging and reproducing failures qualitatively harder than in deterministic software.

runs.text: The operational consequence: the standard software reliability playbook — deploy, observe logs, page on errors — is insufficient for ML systems. You need data quality monitoring, model performance monitoring, and drift detection in addition to the standard observability stack.

Huyen's framing in Designing Machine Learning Systems is precise: ML systems have the properties of traditional software plus additional complexity introduced by data and models. The DevOps practices apply — they are just necessary but not sufficient.

Regular software breaks with an error. ML software breaks quietly — the predictions just get worse because the world changed and the model didn't. That silent degradation is why ML is harder to operate.

cards.title: Sculley et al.: Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems
cards.teaser: The 2015 Google paper "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" by D. Sculley and colleagues is the foundational document for the field. It established that the majority of code in a production ML system is not ML code — and that this surrounding code is where most of the technical debt accumulates.

runs.text: Published at NeurIPS 2015 by D. Sculley, Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, Eugene Davydov, Todd Phillips, Dietmar Ebner, Vinay Chaudhary, Michael Young, Jean-Francois Crespo, and Dan Dennison — all from Google — the paper drew on Google's internal experience operating large-scale ML systems and identified patterns of technical debt that were specific to ML.

The paper's central observation, illustrated with a now-famous diagram: in a real ML production system, the box labeled "ML code" is a small fraction of the total codebase. It is surrounded by a much larger mass of infrastructure code:
Sculley et al. named several specific debt patterns:
entanglement
(changing any input feature changes the model),
glue code
(ad-hoc scripts binding together research libraries),
pipeline jungles
(data preparation code that grew without design),
dead experimental codepaths
(branches from old experiments never cleaned up), and
undeclared consumers
(downstream systems reading model outputs without the model owner's knowledge).

The paper's closing line is often quoted: "ML systems have a special capacity for incurring technical debt." It is the founding document for MLOps as a discipline. Every framework, platform, and practice in the MLOps space is either directly or indirectly a response to the problems it named.

The Sculley paper showed that most of the code in a production ML system is not the ML part — it is all the plumbing around it. That plumbing is where the technical debt piles up, and nobody was paying attention to it.

cards.title: Glue Code: The Small-Fraction Myth
cards.teaser: Sculley et al. named "glue code" as one of the most pervasive sources of technical debt in ML systems. Glue code is the ad-hoc, often untested scripts that stitch together research libraries, data sources, and serving infrastructure. It is where most production ML time is actually spent.

runs.text: The myth of ML work is that it is mostly modeling — selecting architectures, tuning hyperparameters, evaluating metrics. The reality of ML production work is that the modeling is a small fraction of the total effort. The large fraction is glue code.

Glue code arises because ML systems import research frameworks (scikit-learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch, XGBoost) that were not designed for production. Each framework has its own API, serialization format, and prediction interface. Connecting them to a production system — reading features from a feature store, transforming them into the format the model expects, calling predict(), and formatting the result for a downstream consumer — requires hand-written adapter code.
The properties of glue code that make it dangerous:

items.text: Glue code is written quickly to make something work. Tests are skipped because "we'll add them later." Later means never.
The person who wrote the glue code knows why each choice was made. When they leave the team, that knowledge leaves with them.
Glue code written against scikit-learn 0.22 breaks when scikit-learn 1.0 changes an API. Because nobody owns the glue code, upgrades are deferred indefinitely.

The glue code used in training (a Jupyter notebook) and the glue code used in serving (a Flask route) are often written separately, by different people, and diverge over time — causing training-serving skew.

runs.text: The MLOps response to glue code is standardization: shared feature pipelines, typed prediction interfaces, and ML platforms (such as Uber's Michelangelo or Airbnb's Bighead) that enforce consistent patterns so glue code either does not need to be written or is written once and reused.

Glue code is all the untested, undocumented scripting that connects a model to everything around it. It looks like plumbing, but when it breaks or drifts from the training logic, it breaks the whole ML system.

cards.title: Pipeline Jungles
cards.teaser: A pipeline jungle is what Sculley et al. named the data preparation and feature engineering code that grew without intentional design — a tangle of scripts, cron jobs, and manual steps that nobody fully understands, that is dangerous to modify, and that nobody owns.

runs.text: Pipeline jungles are the ML equivalent of the accidental architecture problem in CI/CD. They arise when data scientists need data transformed and write scripts to do it. Each script is local, undocumented, and correct for the moment. Over months, ten scripts become the pipeline. The pipeline has no owner. The order matters but isn't specified. Intermediate outputs are stored in ad-hoc locations. One script reads from a path that another script is responsible for populating, and that dependency is expressed only as an implicit assumption.
The symptoms of a pipeline jungle:

items.text: "I don't know what happens if I change this step" — a sign that the data lineage is unknown.
Training takes multiple days because there are undocumented sequential dependencies that prevent parallelism.
Feature values computed in the pipeline differ from feature values computed at serving time — training-serving skew introduced by two independent implementations of the same logic.
Deleting any script causes something downstream to break — but nobody knows what, so nothing is ever deleted.

runs.text: Sculley et al.'s prescription was to periodically invest in cleaning up pipeline jungles by rewriting them as clean, tested, end-to-end pipelines. Modern ML orchestration frameworks — Apache Airflow, Kubeflow Pipelines, Metaflow (Netflix), and Prefect — exist precisely to provide the structure that prevents jungles from forming in the first place.

A pipeline jungle is not a data engineering problem — it is an ownership problem. Jungles grow when nobody has responsibility for the data pipeline as a production artifact. The engineering intervention is organizational: assign ownership, require documentation, treat the pipeline as production software.
A pipeline jungle is a data prep codebase that grew by addition instead of design — scripts piled on scripts, nobody knows the full picture, and everyone is afraid to change anything.

cards.title: CACE: Change Anything, Change Everything
cards.teaser: CACE — Change Anything, Change Everything — is the principle Sculley et al. used to describe the entanglement problem in ML systems. Because a model is a function of all its training data and features jointly, changing any single input can change the behavior of the entire model in unpredictable ways.

runs.text: In traditional software, the principle of modularity provides isolation: you change module A, and module B is unaffected unless it imports A. In ML systems, modularity at the feature level does not provide the same isolation. The model is a joint function of all features. Adding a new feature, removing an old one, changing a feature's distribution, or changing the training data — all of these can change model behavior globally.
Sculley et al. called this entanglement, and labeled it with the CACE principle as a mnemonic:
Change Anything, Change Everything.
A few concrete manifestations:

items.text: Adding a highly correlated feature can cause the model to down-weight an existing feature it was previously relying on, changing predictions even for users that the new feature is irrelevant to.

Fixing a bug in a data preprocessing step changes the feature distribution the model was trained on. The model performs differently on the corrected data — possibly better, possibly worse, but differently.
An upstream team changes the schema of a table the feature pipeline reads. The feature values change silently. The model's predictions change. No alert fires.

runs.text: The CACE principle has operational consequences: you cannot treat a model's components as independent. Any change to data, features, preprocessing, or the training process must be treated as a potential change to the model's behavior — and must trigger a full re-evaluation, not just a unit test.

CACE is why MLOps treats experiment tracking and model lineage as first-class concerns. If you know the exact data, features, and code that produced a model, you can reason about what changed between a good model and a bad one. Without lineage, CACE makes root-cause analysis nearly impossible.

CACE means that in an ML system, you can't safely change one input in isolation — because the model learned from everything together. Fixing one bug or adding one feature can shift predictions everywhere.

cards.title: Feedback Loops: Direct and Hidden
cards.teaser: Feedback loops in ML systems are not a theoretical concern — they are a production failure mode. A model whose predictions influence the data used to retrain it will drift systematically toward self-reinforcement. Sculley et al. identified both direct feedback loops and hidden feedback loops as sources of hidden technical debt.

runs.text: A feedback loop in an ML system occurs when model predictions influence the distribution of future training data. Because models are retrained on new data, a feedback loop means the model is partially training on its own outputs.
Two categories:

items.text: The model directly affects the data it is trained on. A recommendation model recommends content; users interact with recommended content; future training data is collected from user interactions. The model trained on this data learns to recommend what it already recommended — amplifying existing biases and starving unpopular content of future training signal.

Two separate models interact in a way that creates a feedback loop not visible from either model's perspective. A pricing model affects demand; a demand forecast model uses demand data; the pricing model is retrained on the forecast. Neither model team is aware of the coupling. The system can enter oscillatory or degenerate behavior.

runs.text: Real-world examples of problematic feedback loops:

items.text: that amplify engagement bait because that content was previously shown and clicked on, generating training signal that reinforces its recommendation.

that direct more police resources to neighborhoods that were over-policed in training data, increasing arrest rates in those neighborhoods, producing more training data that confirms the original prediction — a self-fulfilling loop.
that determine who gets credit — and therefore who builds a credit history — affecting the future population the model will be trained on.

runs.text: Feedback loops are difficult to detect because they manifest slowly — model behavior shifts over months, not minutes. Detecting them requires monitoring the distribution of model predictions over time, not just model accuracy metrics.
A feedback loop in ML is when the model's predictions shape the future data it will be trained on — so it slowly starts training itself into a narrower and narrower view of the world.

cards.title: MLOps Inheritances: DevOps and SRE
cards.teaser: MLOps did not invent its foundational practices — it adapted them from DevOps and SRE. Understanding what MLOps inherits (CI/CD, SLOs, observability, blameless postmortems) and what it had to add (data versioning, model registries, drift monitoring) clarifies the scope of the discipline.

runs.text: The DevOps movement, codified by the DORA research and Jez Humble and Gene Kim's work, established that fast, reliable software delivery requires automation, short feedback loops, and shared ownership between development and operations. MLOps imports all of these.
From DevOps, MLOps inherits:

items.text: Applied to ML: automated testing of data pipelines, automated model validation, automated deployment to serving infrastructure. The analog of a unit test for ML is a model evaluation on a held-out dataset; the analog of a failing build is a model that does not pass evaluation thresholds.
Training environments, serving clusters, and feature stores should be version-controlled and reproducible — not manually configured.
Extended in MLOps to cover not just code but data (DVC, Delta Lake), models (model registries), and experiments (MLflow, Weights & Biases).

runs.text: From SRE (Google's Site Reliability Engineering, 2016), MLOps inherits:

items.text: ML systems should have defined SLOs — not just latency and availability, but model quality thresholds ("the recommendation model must achieve at least X% CTR"). An SLO breach triggers the same on-call response as a latency SLO breach.
Metrics, logs, and traces — plus ML-specific signals: prediction distribution, feature drift, data quality scores, and model performance metrics computed against ground-truth labels when available.
The concept of trading reliability for velocity applies to ML retraining: how often can you push a new model to production without exhausting the team's confidence in the system?
When a model degrades in production, the investigation is a systems problem — not a person problem. Who trained the model is less important than what changed in the data, features, or environment.

runs.text: MLOps borrowed CI/CD and automation from DevOps, and borrowed reliability culture (SLOs, monitoring, blameless postmortems) from SRE — then added everything that is unique to software where the behavior is learned from data.

cards.title: Google's MLOps Maturity Levels: 0, 1, and 2
cards.teaser: Google's MLOps whitepaper (2021) defined three maturity levels for ML systems: Level 0 (manual, notebook-driven processes), Level 1 (automated training pipelines), and Level 2 (automated CI/CD pipelines for the ML system itself). Most organizations operate at Level 0.

runs.text: Google's MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning (cloud.google.com, 2021) provides the most widely cited maturity model for ML systems. Its three levels describe the degree to which the ML lifecycle is automated.

items.text: The data scientist trains a model manually, in a notebook or script. The trained model is exported and handed to an engineer who deploys it. Training is infrequent — maybe once when the model is built, and again when performance degradation is noticed. No automated pipeline. No continuous training. No automated evaluation. This is the default state for most ML projects.

Training is automated as a pipeline. New data triggers automatic retraining and evaluation. The model is deployed automatically if it passes evaluation thresholds. The pipeline is version-controlled. Feature engineering is part of the pipeline, enabling consistent training-serving behavior. The pipeline itself is still deployed manually.

The pipeline itself is treated as software with a CI/CD process. Changes to the pipeline code are automatically built, tested, and deployed. Multiple teams can iterate on models and pipelines independently. This is the level at which organizations like Google, Uber, and Netflix operate.

runs.text: The maturity levels are not a performance ranking — a Level 0 process is appropriate for an exploratory ML project. They are a diagnostic tool: they describe the operational posture of a system and predict where effort is needed as the system scales.

The transition from Level 0 to Level 1 requires building and owning a training pipeline. The transition from Level 1 to Level 2 requires a platform team that treats the pipeline as production software. Most organizations underestimate the organizational investment each transition requires.

Google's three MLOps levels tell you how automated your ML system is: Level 0 is a data scientist retraining manually, Level 1 is an automated training pipeline, and Level 2 is a CI/CD system for the pipeline itself.

cards.title: ResearchOps vs ProductionOps: The Cultural Gap
cards.teaser: The hardest part of deploying ML systems is not technical — it is cultural. Data scientists optimize for model accuracy and experimentation speed. Engineers optimize for reliability, reproducibility, and operability. These goals are not opposed, but they require deliberate alignment to coexist.

runs.text: Andriy Burkov's Machine Learning Engineering frames the cultural gap clearly: a data scientist's definition of "done" is a model with good validation metrics. An engineer's definition of "done" is a system that serves predictions reliably under production load, degrades gracefully, can be updated safely, and can be debugged when something goes wrong. These are different definitions of done, and both are correct for their context.
The cultural gap manifests in specific ways:

items.text: Data scientists work in notebook environments where installing a package is a one-line command. Engineers need that environment specified in a requirements file, container, or conda environment — because production needs to reproduce it. The notebook works on the data scientist's machine. The container must work everywhere.

Research code is exploratory: try things, discard what doesn't work, iterate fast. Production code must be maintainable, tested, and documented. The transition from research code to production code is not a cleanup step — it is often a rewrite.

A data scientist cares about AUC, F1, RMSE. A product manager cares about revenue, user engagement, churn. An engineer cares about p99 latency and uptime. All three metrics matter for a production ML system, and none of them is a proxy for the others.

The model-toss-over-the-wall pattern — where a data scientist trains a model and hands a pickle file to engineering — is where most of the production gap originates. The data scientist has moved on; the engineer does not understand the model's assumptions; neither owns the production system.

runs.text: Successful MLOps organizations bridge this gap through shared platforms (Uber's Michelangelo, Airbnb's Bighead) that give data scientists production-grade tooling with minimal operational burden, and through embedded ML engineers who own the gap between research and production jointly with the data science team.

Data scientists think they are done when the model is accurate. Engineers think the work begins when the model is accurate. MLOps is the practice that closes the gap between those two definitions of done.

cards.title: Where MLOps Fails
cards.teaser: MLOps initiatives fail in predictable ways: teams are undertooled, ownership is undefined, and the model is confused with the system. Understanding these failure modes is the most practical preparation for avoiding them.

runs.text: MLOps adoption is not uniformly successful. Organizations that invest in MLOps tooling and frameworks still encounter the same production failures. Three failure modes account for the majority of MLOps-related production incidents:

items.text: The organization purchased an MLOps platform (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML) but data scientists and ML engineers do not have the training, time, or permissions to use it. The platform sits idle; teams continue working in notebooks and hand-rolling scripts. Tooling adoption requires organizational investment, not just procurement.

No one owns the production ML system end-to-end. The data scientist owns the model. The data engineer owns the feature pipeline. The platform team owns the serving infrastructure. When the system fails, each team investigates their component and finds nothing wrong. The failure lives in the interface between components — where nobody has ownership.

Teams focus ML reliability efforts on the model: evaluation metrics, bias testing, robustness checks. The model passes all checks. The system still fails because the feature pipeline has a bug, the serving infrastructure is misconfigured, or an upstream data source changed schema. The model is a component of the system. System reliability requires operating the whole system, not just the model in isolation.

runs.text: A fourth failure mode specific to mature organizations:
over-engineering.

Teams build Level 2 MLOps infrastructure for a problem that requires one model, retrained quarterly. The infrastructure cost exceeds the value delivered. MLOps is not a single target state — it is a set of practices applied at the appropriate level of sophistication for the actual problem.

The most common single-point-of-failure in production ML is undefined ownership of the training-serving boundary. Establish explicit ownership of the production ML system — not the model, not the pipeline, but the system — before any other MLOps investment.

MLOps fails most often in three ways: the tools exist but nobody uses them, nobody owns the full system end-to-end, or teams focus on the model and ignore everything around it. All three are organizational problems, not technical ones.

cards.title: ML Platforms in the Wild: Michelangelo, Bighead, and Metaflow
cards.teaser: The first generation of internal ML platforms at Uber, Airbnb, and Netflix proved the value of MLOps at scale — and their public descriptions became the blueprints for the commercial MLOps tools that followed. Understanding what they solved clarifies what MLOps is for.

runs.text: Between 2015 and 2019, several large technology companies reached the same conclusion independently: getting ML into production at scale required a shared internal platform, not a collection of individual team practices. Three of the most influential:

items.text: (described publicly in 2017): a unified platform covering the full ML lifecycle — data management, model training, model evaluation, model deployment, and prediction serving. Before Michelangelo, Uber had dozens of disconnected ML workflows. After: a common platform that enabled scaling from dozens to hundreds of models with consistent operational practices.

(described publicly in 2019): Airbnb's answer to the same problem, with particular focus on reproducible experimentation and seamless transition from research to production. Bighead introduced the concept of the "ML project" as a first-class artifact with versioned code, data, and configurations.

(open-sourced in 2019): a Python-native framework for defining ML workflows as code, with built-in versioning, resource management, and integration with AWS infrastructure. Metaflow's key design insight: data scientists should write Python, not YAML. The framework handles orchestration, scaling, and artifact management transparently.

runs.text: All three platforms solved the same core problems: eliminating glue code, preventing pipeline jungles, enforcing training-serving consistency, and providing observability into production models. Their public descriptions established the vocabulary and architecture patterns that shaped the entire MLOps tooling ecosystem — Kubeflow, MLflow, SageMaker, Vertex AI, and Weights & Biases all reflect design choices pioneered in these internal platforms.

Uber, Airbnb, and Netflix each built their own internal MLOps platforms because no off-the-shelf solution existed. Their designs — Michelangelo, Bighead, and Metaflow — became the blueprints for every commercial MLOps tool that followed.

cards.title: The 2026 Inflection: LLMs and the Rise of LLMOps
cards.teaser: The wide availability of large language models starting in 2023 did not replace traditional MLOps — it accelerated its adoption and introduced a subdiscipline: LLMOps. LLMs brought new operational challenges (prompt engineering, hallucination monitoring, context window management, cost control) that required extending the MLOps playbook.

runs.text: The release of ChatGPT in late 2022 and the subsequent enterprise adoption of LLMs through 2023–2026 forced every organization to confront MLOps problems that were previously confined to large tech companies. Deploying an LLM-backed feature is not fundamentally different from deploying any ML system — but LLMs introduced new dimensions of operational complexity.
What LLMs changed:

items.text: Cost is a first-class operational metric.

LLM inference costs are orders of magnitude higher than traditional model inference. MLOps monitoring for LLM systems must track token consumption, cost per request, and cost-quality tradeoffs — not just latency and throughput.

The CACE principle applies to prompts: change a system prompt and the model's behavior changes globally. Prompts must be version-controlled, tested against evaluation suites, and deployed through the same pipeline discipline applied to model artifacts.

Traditional ML has ground-truth labels. LLM outputs are often open-ended text whose quality is difficult to evaluate automatically. LLMOps requires LLM-as-judge evaluation patterns, human feedback collection pipelines, and hallucination detection.

Most production LLM systems are not raw LLMs — they are LLMs combined with retrieval systems. This introduces a second ML component (the embedding model and vector search) that requires its own operational lifecycle, drift monitoring, and reindexing pipeline.

runs.text: The term LLMOps emerged in 2023 and refers to the operationalization practices specific to LLM-backed systems. It is MLOps extended — not MLOps replaced. The pipeline, monitoring, versioning, and ownership principles of MLOps remain foundational. LLMOps adds the tooling and practices specific to the unique properties of language models.

By 2026, LLM adoption had made MLOps concerns visible at organizations that previously had no ML in production. The 87% never-deployed statistic applies to LLM applications as directly as to traditional models — the infrastructure gap is the same, even if the models are accessed via API rather than trained in-house.

LLMs didn't replace MLOps — they forced every company to face the same operational problems that big tech faced with traditional ML. LLMOps is MLOps with extra problems: prompts need versioning, outputs are hard to evaluate automatically, and inference costs a lot of money.
